name: Chupacabra
description: THE MOST FAMOUS modern cryptid — first reported March 1995 in Puerto Rico. Name = Spanish 'chupa' (sucks) + 'cabra' (goat) = 'Goat-Sucker.' Before this, the 1975 'vampiro de Moca' attacked livestock in the town of Moca, initially suspected as Satanic cult activity, then reclassified as a 'vampire.' The name was coined by comedian Silverio Pérez in 1995. The Canóvanas eyewitness Madelyne Tolentino described a creature 4-5 feet tall with large wraparound eyes, gray skin, and spines down its back — which became the classic description. Skeptics note that the film Species (1995) featuring the alien 'Sil' premiered the same year. Attacks escalated rapidly: 8 sheep in March 1995, then 150+ animals with puncture wounds in the neck and all blood drained. By 1996, reports spread throughout Mexico, Brazil, Chile, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Panama, Peru, and the USA. TWO distinct types emerged: (1) Bipedal — reptilian kangaroo with spines (the 'classic'); (2) Quadruped — hairless dog-like (later proved to be mangy coyotes/dogs). In the US Southwest, dozens of alleged Chupacabra carcasses were reported across Texas — in San Antonio, Cuero, Hood County, and Coleman County. The infamous 'Cuero Chupacabra' (2007) gained national attention before DNA tests revealed a coyote-wolf hybrid with severe sarcoptic mange. Cryptozoologist Benjamin Radford's 2011 investigation concluded the real attacks were predators with disease, circular wounds from carnivorous animals — not a vampire. Yet the stories persist, demonstrating how folklore evolves in real time
source: Puerto Rican/Latin American folklore — the Chupacabra goat-sucker cryptid documented since the 1990s.

name: Chupacabras Boricua
description: Chupacabras Boricua is the Puerto Rican regional variant of the legendary Chupacabra cryptid, distinguished by its specific origin in the island's folklore and unique description compared to mainland versions. The name Boricua refers to the Taino name for Puerto Rico, Boriken, making this the original version of the Chupacabra legend that emerged in 1995. The first reported attack occurred in March 1995 in Moca, Puerto Rico, where eight sheep were found dead with puncture wounds and reportedly drained of blood. The name chupacabras meaning goat-sucker was coined by Puerto Rican comedian Silverio Perez. The most famous eyewitness Madelyne Tolentino of Canovanas reported seeing the creature in August 1995, and her description became the template for the Puerto Rican version, later investigated extensively by skeptic Benjamin Radford
source: Puerto Rican folklore — the Chupacabra goat-sucker documented in Puerto Rican oral tradition.

name: Chupacora
description: Chupacora is a lesser-known regional variant of the Chupacabra legend documented primarily in rural areas of Central America and northern South America, particularly in Honduras, Nicaragua, and Colombia. While sharing the core characteristic of attacking livestock, the Chupacora has distinct local features that differentiate it from both the Puerto Rican reptilian version and the mainland dog-like version. The name appears to be a regional corruption of chupacabras influenced by local dialects. The Chupacora legend emerged in the late 1990s as Chupacabra reports spread southward from Mexico into South America. The creature is part of a broader phenomenon of livestock mutilation reports that swept through Latin America, often coinciding with droughts or economic hardships that focused community anxiety on mysterious external threats
source: Guatemalan folklore — La Chupacabra variant documented in Guatemalan oral tradition.

name: Ciguapa
description: The Ciguapa is a nocturnal mythical creature from Dominican folklore, described as a wild woman who inhabits the high mountain regions of the island. Her most distinctive feature is that her feet are turned backward, making it nearly impossible for hunters or trackers to follow her footprints. She is deeply tied to the natural world, possessing expert knowledge of medicinal herbs and plants found in the dense tropical forests. The first written account of the Ciguapa appeared in 1866 in the story 'La Ciguapa' by Francisco Javier Angulo Guridi. Some scholars debate whether the legend has Taíno origins or was introduced through European influences, drawing comparisons to mermaid myths and the Hindu churel In Dominican Republic folklore, this figure is known among the Dominican Republic people.
source: Dominican republic mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Cipitío
description: Cipitío is a beloved legendary character from Salvadoran folklore, the illegitimate son of La Siguanaba and Lucero de la Mañana (Lucifer). Cursed by the god Teotl as a result of his mother's infidelity, he was condemned to remain a child forever, with his feet set backward as a reminder of the twisted affair of his parents. He is generally portrayed as an 8 to 10-year-old boy with a large conical hat and a pot belly. His name derives from the Nahuatl word 'cipit' or 'cipote' meaning child. Cipitío is a mischievous trickster who wanders into farmers' fields, throws pebbles at beautiful women, hides in bushes to scare people, and eats ashes leftover in rural kitchens. Farmers would find child's footprints in their fields and blame Cipitío. Despite his mischief, he is generally regarded as benevolent and is even associated with bringing good luck. He is so beloved that he has his own television show on Salvadoran Educational Television, where he teaches morals and values to children
source: Salvadoran oral tradition; snip Wikipedia (Cipitio); snip USC Digital Folklore Archives; snip El Salvador Tips

name: Comorian Jinn (Mashetani)
aliases: Jinn of the Isles of the Moon
description: In the Comoros Islands, belief in jinn (locally called mashetani) is deeply ingrained in the culture, representing a syncretic blend of Islamic theology with indigenous African and Malagasy spirit beliefs. Comorian jinn are invisible spirits created from smokeless fire who inhabit a parallel world to humans. They are believed to dwell in specific locations such as ancient baobab trees, volcanic craters, coral reefs, and abandoned wells. Unlike the purely malevolent spirits found in some traditions, Comorian jinn are morally complex beings capable of both good and evil actions. They are particularly associated with illness and strange behavior, and traditional healers (fundi or mganga) perform rituals to diagnose and treat jinn-related afflictions. The belief system reflects the islands' history as a crossroads of Swahili-Arabic culture, where maritime trade brought not only goods but also spiritual concepts from across the Indian Ocean. Respect for jinn involves specific protocols: avoiding whistling at night, seeking permission before entering certain areas, and leaving offerings of food or incense
source: IslaGuru; New Lines Magazine; Comorian oral traditions

name: Conjure Doctor
description: The Conjure Doctor (also known as a root doctor, hoodoo doctor, or two-headed doctor) is a powerful figure in African American folk belief — a practitioner of conjure, hoodoo, and rootwork who possesses supernatural knowledge and the ability to influence events through magical means. Conjure Doctors serve as community healers, spiritual advisors, and protectors against evil. They use herbs, roots, bones, and personal items to create mojo bags, cast spells, or provide protection. Essential tools include John the Conqueror root (for luck and protection), goofer dust (for cursing), black cat bones (for invisibility and luck), and candles. The Conjure Doctor occupies an ambiguous position — feared for their power to curse, respected for their power to heal, and essential to the spiritual life of the community
source: Zora Neale Hurston, Mules and Men (1935)

name: Coqui (Sacred Frog Spirit of Puerto Rico)
description: The Coqui is a tiny tree frog (Eleutherodactylus coqui) native to Puerto Rico that has transcended biology to become a sacred cultural and mythological symbol. In Taino mythology, the Coqui distinctive two-note nocturnal call Co-kee! has a divine origin. According to legend, a beautiful Taino goddess fell in love with Coqui, the chief son. They met in secret, but the evil god Juracan (the spirit of chaos and hurricanes) snatched Coqui away. Heartbroken, the goddess transformed her lover into a tiny frog that would forever call his own name into the night. The Taino people depicted the Coqui extensively in petroglyphs, pottery, and stone carvings, with its wide-eyed frog symbol representing fertility, femaleness, and the spirit world. Today, the Coqui is an unofficial national symbol of Puerto Rico -- the saying Soy de aqui, como el coqui (I am from here, like the coqui) expresses deep-rooted cultural identity
source: Taino / Puerto Rican oral tradition, Puerto Rico folklore

name: Cosmic Elk
description: The Cosmic Elk (also called the Golden-antlered Deer or Celestial Elk) is a central figure in Sami astral mythology — the great elk or reindeer that lives in the sky and is hunted by the thunder god Horagalles (Tiermes/Dierpmis). This cosmic hunt is reflected in the constellations: Orion is the hunter, the Pleiades are the deer/elk, and the Milky Way is the tracks of the mythic elk-hunter's skis. When the thunder god shoots the celestial elk with his fiery arrow, an apocalypse ensues — fire envelops the earth, mountains boil, ice boils, stars fall, the moon goes out, and the sun sinks. The myth is described in Kola Sami tradition: 'But on earth it becomes dust.' Petroglyphs from the last millennium BC depict this cosmic hunt myth, showing its ancient origins. The golden-antlered deer is sometimes identified with Meandash-pyyrre, the celestial form of the mythic reindeer who is also described as a sun symbol, the snow-covered golden-horned reindeer who flies from one side of the land to the other
source: folklore.ee; Pentikäinen 1995; Ylimartimo, Daughter of the Sun; OAPEN

name: Cougar Deity (Muisca)
description: In Muisca mythology of the Colombian Altiplano Cundiboyacense, the cougar (puma) held profound spiritual significance as a deity associated with the underworld, caves, and the passage between earthly and spiritual realms. The Muisca people, who inhabited the highlands of present-day Bogota before the Spanish conquest, believed that cougars served as guardians of sacred cave entrances leading to the underworld known as the House of the Dead. The cougar was closely tied to Bachue, the mother goddess who emerged from Lake Iguaque with a baby in her arms, and who later transformed into a serpent to return to the underworld. Muisca priests and shamans performed rituals invoking the cougar spirit during initiations and funerary ceremonies, believing the cat's power could guide souls through the dangerous transitions between life and death. The cougar's cave-dwelling nature made it a natural symbol of the hidden mysteries beneath the earth
source: Regional folk beliefs and indigenous cosmology of South America, documented in Andean and Amazonian ethnographic records.

name: Cougar Deity of Maliseet
description: In Maliseet (Wolastoqiyik) tradition, the cougar holds a place of spiritual significance as a guardian of the sky world and a mediator between earthly and celestial realms. The Maliseet are part of the Wabanaki Confederacy, indigenous peoples of northeastern North America whose territory spans present-day New Brunswick, Quebec, and Maine. In Maliseet cosmology, the cougar is associated with Koluskap (also known as Glooscap), the great transformer and culture hero who shaped the world and taught humans how to live. The cougar is one of the animal spirits who assisted Koluskap in his works and watches over the Wabanaki people from its place among the stars. Traditional Maliseet elders recount stories of the cougar as a silent guardian of the forests and mountains, a being whose wisdom was sought by those undertaking vision quests or seeking spiritual guidance in times of communal crisis
source: Indigenous North American folk beliefs and ethnographic records, including academic studies of Native American spiritual traditions.

name: Cougar Deity of Paiute
description: In Paiute oral tradition, the cougar (mountain lion) holds a complex role as both a powerful spirit being and a character in the mythic cycles of the Numic peoples of the Great Basin. The Paiute, whose traditional territory spans the arid regions of Nevada, Utah, California, Oregon, Idaho, and Arizona, maintained an intricate cosmology where animal spirits played crucial roles in creation stories and moral teachings. The cougar appears in Paiute legends as a formidable ally who helped the Shoshone-Bannock people defeat the warlike Nimerigar, the cannibalistic little people of Paiute and Shoshone folklore. In this tale, the cougar spirit joins Wolf, Fox, and Bobcat to vanquish these dangerous beings and restore safety to the people. The Paiute believed that mountain lions possessed special powers of stealth and protection, and their claws and teeth were used in medicine bundles by shamans
source: Indigenous North American folk beliefs and ethnographic records, including academic studies of Native American spiritual traditions.

name: Cougar Deity of Yoruba
description: In Yoruba cosmology, the cougar as a concept merges with the symbolic significance of ekun (leopard), the great feline predator that represents royalty, power, and spiritual authority throughout Yorubaland in present-day Nigeria and Benin. While cougars are not native to West Africa, the Yoruba peoples recognition of great felines as spiritual beings extends to all large wild cats, including the panther. In Yoruba tradition, the leopard is the totem of royalty, associated with the Oba (king) and with the thunder deity Shango, who is often depicted wearing leopard skin and wielding a double-headed axe. The Yoruba consider the leopard a hot, aggressive animal associated with the color red, symbolizing both the kings fearsome power and the balanced temperament a ruler must maintain between hot aggression and cool wisdom. Ifa divination poetry contains numerous references to ekun as a symbol of supreme authority
source: Regional folk beliefs and indigenous cosmology of West Africa, documented in ethnographic surveys of the Akan, Yoruba, Dogon, and Igbo cultures.

name: Cougar Ghost of Choctaw
description: In Choctaw tradition, the cougar ghost is a spirit-being associated with the protection of waterways and rivers, domains connected to the underworld and the great serpent of Choctaw mythology. The Choctaw people, originally from the southeastern United States in present-day Mississippi, Alabama, and Louisiana, maintained a rich spiritual tradition in which animal spirits served as guardians of specific territories and natural features. The panther (cougar) was one of the major clan animals among the Choctaw, belonging to the Panther clan, one of the totemic iksa (clan) designations. The cougar ghost is specifically linked to river crossings and water boundaries, acting as a guardian at the threshold between the world of the living and the domain of the great horned serpent Sinti lapitta, a powerful water spirit with the head of a panther and the body of a snake. The cougar ghost ensures that those who cross rivers do so with proper respect
source: Choctaw spiritual tradition; documented in Southeastern indigenous records.

name: Cougar Ghost of Lakota
description: In Lakota oral tradition, the cougar (ignika or mountain lion) is a powerful spirit associated with the desert and arid lands, serving as a guardian of sacred sites in the Badlands and Black Hills. The Lakota people, part of the Oceti Sakowin (Seven Council Fires) of the Great Sioux Nation, historically inhabited the northern Great Plains. In Lakota cosmology, the mountain lion is one of the powerful animal spirits that medicine people and warriors seek in vision quests, offering gifts of stealth, patience, and strategic wisdom. The cougar holds a distinctive place in Lakota spirituality as a spirit of solitary power and silent observation. The Lakota distinguish between the cougar and other predators like the wolf (which represents family and community) and the bear (which represents healing and strength), seeing the cougar as representing the lone warrior path, the individual who must stand apart to protect the whole. Cougar hides were used in sacred bundles
source: Lakota spiritual tradition; documented in Plains indigenous ethnographic records.

name: Cougar Giant of Choctaw
description: In Choctaw oral tradition, the cougar giant is a colossal underground spirit-being that dwells beneath the earth, connected to the Choctaw emergence myth and the sacred mound of Nanih Waiya. According to Choctaw tradition, their ancestors emerged from the underworld through the great mound Nanih Waiya, a sacred earthwork in present-day Mississippi. The cougar giant is one of the primordial beings that dwell in the caverns beneath the mound, serving as a guardian of the passage between the underworld and the surface world. This being is distinct from the cougar ghost that guards rivers, representing instead the raw telluric forces of the earth itself. The cougar giant is associated with the Choctaw belief that powerful spirits inhabit the underground realm, and that the stability of the world above depends on maintaining harmony with these subterranean powers. Earthquakes and cave-ins were attributed to the cougar giants movements deep below
source: Choctaw spiritual tradition; documented in Southeastern indigenous records.

name: Cougar Giant of Kikuyu
description: In Kikuyu (Gikuyu) traditions of Kenya, the cougar as a distinct concept does not exist since cougars are not native to Africa, but the cougar giant represents the powerful feline spirits that guard the lakes and water bodies of the Kikuyu highlands, particularly the sacred waters of the Mount Kenya region. In Kikuyu cosmology, Ngai (Mwene Nyaga), the supreme god, dwells atop Mount Kenya (Kirinyaga), and the mountains lakes and tarns are considered sacred spaces where the divine touches the earth. The marozi or spotted lion of the Aberdare Mountains, a cryptid reported in Kikuyu oral tradition, shares characteristics with the cougar giant concept. Kikuyu folklore tells of giant spirit cats that guard the glacial lakes on Mount Kenya, creatures that are neither lion nor leopard but something else entirely, beings that have watched over the waters since the time of Gikuyu and Mumbi, the first parents of the Kikuyu people
source: Regional survey of East African indigenous traditions — Kikuyu, Luo, Ganda, Chaga, Malagasy, Maasai, Somali, Ethiopian, and related peoples as documented in regional ethnographic surveys and oral literature collections.

name: Cougar Giant of Kwakiutl
description: In Kwakiutl (Kwakwaka'wakw) tradition from the Pacific Northwest Coast of British Columbia, the cougar giant is a spirit-being associated with the steep cliffs and coastal mountain forests of Kwakwaka'wakw territory. The Kwakwaka'wakw have a rich pantheon of spirit beings including Dzunukwa the wild woman of the woods, Bakwas the ghost king, and the powerful sea serpent Sisiutl. Within this cosmology, the cougar giant represents the untamed power of the coastal mountains, a solitary hunter that roams the cliff faces and old-growth forests between the villages. The cougar giant is one of the transformation beings that appear in the winter ceremonials, where dancers embody spirit powers through elaborate masks and regalia. In Kwakwaka'wakw oral tradition, the cougar giant is sometimes associated with the mountains that separate the coastal villages from the interior, serving as an intermediary between the sea and sky realms
source: Indigenous North American oral traditions — spirits and beings documented across Native American and First Nations folklore as collected in standard ethnographic sources (Curtis, Boas, Mooney, Schoolcraft, collections of the Bureau of American Ethnology).

name: Cougar Giant of Shoshone
description: In Shoshone oral tradition, the cougar giant is a powerful spirit-being associated with the vast open skies of the Great Basin and Rocky Mountains, serving as a guardian of the mountain passes and sky world. The Shoshone people traditionally inhabited a vast territory spanning present-day Nevada, Utah, Idaho, Wyoming, and California. Shoshone cosmology features Wolf (Esa) as the creator and culture hero, with Coyote as his trickster brother. Among the animal spirits that assist Wolf in his works, the cougar holds a special place as a hunter spirit and guardian of the northern and eastern mountain ranges. The cougar appears prominently in the Shoshone-Bannock legend The Wolf, the Fox, the Bobcat and the Cougar, where these four animal spirits join forces to defeat the cannibalistic Nimerigar little people who terrorized the Shoshone bands, establishing the cougar as a protector of the people against supernatural threats
source: Indigenous North American oral traditions — spirits and beings documented across Native American and First Nations folklore as collected in standard ethnographic sources (Curtis, Boas, Mooney, Schoolcraft, collections of the Bureau of American Ethnology).

name: Cougar Giant of Ute
description: In Ute oral tradition, the cougar giant (mountain lion) is a powerful spirit being associated with the underground world and the earths hidden powers, serving as a guardian of the subterranean realm and the sacred springs that emerge from it. The Ute people, who have inhabited the Rocky Mountains and Colorado Plateau for thousands of years, maintain a cosmology where the earth is animated by powerful spirits, with the mountain lion being one of the most significant. In Ute mythology, Sinawav (the creator) shaped the world and gave the mountain lion domain over the mountainous regions, particularly the San Juan Mountains which the Ute consider sacred. The mountain lion is identified with the color yellow and the summer season, representing the mountaintops where the sunrise first touches. Ute tradition holds that the mountain lion spirit, along with the eagle, wolf, bear, and weasel, are the major animal-spirits that maintain balance in the cosmos
source: Indigenous North American oral traditions — spirits and beings documented across Native American and First Nations folklore as collected in standard ethnographic sources (Curtis, Boas, Mooney, Schoolcraft, collections of the Bureau of American Ethnology).

name: Cougar Guardian of Aymara
description: In Aymara cosmology from the Andean highlands of Bolivia, Peru, and Chile, the cougar guardian (puma) is a sacred animal spirit associated with mountain springs, water sources, and the pastoral economy that sustains Aymara communities. The Aymara people, who have inhabited the altiplano around Lake Titicaca for millennia, consider the puma one of the most spiritually significant animals in their religious system. In Aymara tradition, the puma belongs to a group of eight sacred emblematic animals known as sallka (wild animals that are loved), each associated with specific productive functions in the Andean world. The puma and the chullumpe bird are emblems of pastoralism, serving as spiritual pastors for llamas and alpacas. The Aymara believe that mountain spirits (mallkus) appointed the puma as their awatiri (pastor), the supernatural shepherd of the wild herds that belong to the mountain gods
source: Regional folk beliefs and indigenous cosmology of South America, documented in Andean and Amazonian ethnographic records.

name: Cougar Guardian of Baloch
description: In Baloch folklore from the regions of Pakistan, Iran, and Afghanistan, the cougar guardian is associated with the protection of caves and mountain refuges, drawing on the broader Persianate tradition of big cat symbolism that permeates the mythology of the Iranian plateau. While cougars are not native to Balochistan, the concept merges with figures like the palang (panther) and babr (tiger), which appear extensively in Persian and Balochi epic poetry and folk tales. In Balochi oral tradition, the mountain cat spirit is a guardian of hidden caves, treasure sites, and sacred springs in the rugged terrain of Balochistan. The Baloch people, who have historically been nomadic pastoralists and traders, tell stories of a great cave cat that protects ancient strongholds and the spirits of Baloch heroes buried in the mountains. This guardian is connected to pre-Islamic Zoroastrian traditions of animal spirits that serve as protectors of sacred places
source: Regional survey of South Asian folklore and mythology — Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, and indigenous traditions of India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, and Bhutan as documented in sacred texts and regional folklore collections.

name: Cougar Guardian of Creek
description: In Creek (Muscogee) tradition, the cougar guardian is associated with the protection of the oceans and large water bodies, reflecting the Creek peoples historical territory along the Gulf Coast and Atlantic seaboard of the southeastern United States. The Creek Confederacy, comprising numerous Muscogee-speaking towns, maintained a complex cosmology in which the cosmos is divided into three worlds: the Upper World, the Middle World, and the Lower World. The cougar guardian patrols the boundary between the Middle World of humans and the Lower World of water spirits. The Creek Panther clan (Katsalgi or Kaccvlke) is one of the principal clans, and members of this clan traditionally served as the medicine makers and spiritual leaders of Creek towns. The Seminole people, who split from the Creek, also maintain the Panther clan as the premier medicinal clan, with the panther being the first creature to emerge onto the earth during creation
source: Indigenous North American folk beliefs and ethnographic records, including academic studies of Native American spiritual traditions.

name: Cougar Guardian of Mapuche
description: In Mapuche tradition from Chile and Argentina, the cougar guardian (pangui in Mapudungun) is a powerful spirit-being associated with the underworld and the protection of sacred mountains and underground passages. The Mapuche people, who have inhabited the southern Andes for millennia, regard the puma as one of their most significant spiritual animals. The puma is called futamaye meaning great uncle in Mapudungun, reflecting the close relationship between the Mapuche people and this powerful feline. Mapuche warriors traditionally incorporated particles of puma bone into their bodies during initiation ceremonies to gain the cats strength and courage. The cougar guardian protects the entrances to the underworld (Minche Mapu), the realm beneath the earth where Mapuche spirits reside after death. The Mapuche believe that the puma spirit acts as an intermediary between the human world and the spirits of the ancestors who dwell below
source: Regional folk beliefs and indigenous cosmology of South America, documented in Andean and Amazonian ethnographic records.

name: Coyote Ancestor-Spirit of Navajo
description: Known as Mą'ii in the Navajo language, the Coyote ancestor-spirit is one of the most complex and revered figures in Diné Bahane', the Navajo creation story. Unlike lesser spirits, Mą'ii existed from the beginning of time, present in the First World of darkness and mist alongside First Man and First Woman. He is both a creator and a destroyer, a teacher and a trickster, whose ceremonial name is Áłtsé hashké or First Scolder. Coyote's actions during the emergence from the underworlds shaped the very fabric of the world as the Navajo know it today. He scattered the stars into the Milky Way when he grew impatient with Black God's careful placement, stole Water Buffalo's children causing the great flood, and introduced both death and the monthly cycles into human existence through his arguments against the simplicity of eternal daylight
source: Indigenous North American folklore; Coyote is a widespread trickster and culture hero.

name: Coyote Deity of Haida
description: In Haida mythology from the Haida Gwaii archipelago, the coyote deity is a lesser-known figure compared to the central trickster Raven, yet it holds a distinct role as a terrestrial counterpart to the sky-dwelling Raven. While Raven (Yáahl) brought light, fresh water, and humans from the clamshell, the coyote deity is credited with shaping the land itself, carving out the inlets, fjords, and beaches of the Pacific Northwest coast through its endless digging and burrowing. In some Haida traditions, the coyote and Raven are considered brothers, one ruling the sky and the other the earth, their perpetual rivalry and cooperation creating the balance of the natural world. This deity is particularly associated with the cedar forests and the underground root systems that hold the coastal mountains together
source: Indigenous North American folklore; Coyote is a widespread trickster and culture hero.

name: Coyote Deity of Miwok
description: In Miwok mythology of Northern California, Coyote is one of the most important and revered figures, serving as both the creator god and the ultimate trickster. According to Miwok creation stories, in the beginning there was only water until Silver Fox, a female creator spirit, sang a song of loneliness and Coyote answered. Together they danced and sang the world into existence, creating the earth beneath their feet through the power of their creative expression. Coyote is the ancestor of the Miwok people, their creator god who shaped the first humans from feathers of crow and buzzard, modeling their hands after the five fingers of Lizard. He breathed life into them and gave them acorns, fire, and the knowledge of social organization, establishing the foundations of Miwok society in the Sierra Nevada and the California coastal ranges
source: Indigenous North American folklore; Coyote is a widespread trickster and culture hero.

name: Coyote Ghost of Kazakh
description: In Kazakh folklore, where the vast steppes of Central Asia stretch endlessly beneath an ancient sky, the coyote ghost appears as a restless spirit known as the Iyt-Köz, or dog-eyed wanderer. Unlike the totemic wolf revered by Turkic peoples as the legendary ancestor of all Turkic nations, the coyote ghost represents the marginalized trickster, the spirit that survives on the edges of settlements and the boundaries of civilization. Kazakh nomadic traditions speak of this spirit as the remnant of a shaman who failed to pass properly into the afterlife, condemned to wander the steppes between the worlds of the living and the dead. It is particularly active during the harsh winter months when the boundary between worlds grows thin and the spirits of the ancestors draw close to the felt yurts of the nomadic Kazakh people
source: Kazakh folklore — spirit figure from Kazakh oral tradition.

name: Coyote Ghost of Yurok
description: In Yurok mythology from the lower Klamath River region of northwestern California, the coyote ghost is an ambivalent spirit associated with the sky world and the celestial realm where the White Deerskin Dance is performed eternally. Yurok cosmology describes the sky as containing a great river of stars, and at the head of this river dwells a gigantic white coyote and its yellow mate, guardians of the celestial deer that are the source of all earthly deer. The coyote ghost of Yurok tradition is distinct from the trickster figure Wohpekumew, the culture hero who emerged from across the ocean to teach the Yurok people. Instead, this ghost represents the spirit of the nocturnal coyote, the one that howls at the moon and guards the boundary between the daily world of fishing and gathering and the sacred world of ceremony and spiritual renewal
source: Indigenous North American folklore; Coyote is a widespread trickster and culture hero.

name: Coyote Giant of Yurok
description: In Yurok oral traditions from the Pacific Coast of Northern California, the coyote giant is a primordial being that belongs to the age before the current world was established, when animals and spirits had not yet separated into their present forms. Yurok narratives speak of a time when the earth was populated by giant beings who shaped the landscape through their actions, and the coyote giant was one of the most significant of these figures. Unlike the celestial white coyote that guards the sky world, the coyote giant is an earth-bound force that carved the redwood forests and the Klamath River canyon through its immense size and strength. When the world was reorganized and the current order established, the coyote giant was transformed into the spirit of the old-growth forests, its body becoming the hills and its fur becoming the ferns and mosses that carpet the forest floor of Yurok ancestral territory
source: Indigenous North American folklore; Coyote is a widespread trickster and culture hero.

name: Coyote Guardian of Baloch
description: In Baloch folklore from the arid regions of Pakistan, Iran, and Afghanistan, the coyote guardian is a spirit of the rocky cliffs and mountain passes that protect the hidden water sources of the Makran coast and the Sulaiman Mountains. The Baloch people, with their rich tradition of oral poetry and storytelling, describe this guardian as the Gurg-e-Koh, the wolf of the mountains, though it shares more characteristics with the coyote than the true wolves that once roamed these ranges. This spirit is particularly associated with the hoshk, the dry riverbeds that flood suddenly during the rare rains, and it is said to guard the ancient knowledge of where underground water can be found during the long droughts that shape life in Balochistan. The coyote guardian is respected by both settled farmers and nomadic herders, who leave offerings at cairns built on mountain passes to ensure safe passage through the harsh terrain
source: Regional survey of South Asian folklore and mythology — Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, and indigenous traditions of India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, and Bhutan as documented in sacred texts and regional folklore collections.

name: Coyote Guardian of Cheyenne
description: In Cheyenne mythology from the Great Plains, the coyote guardian holds a position of profound significance as a spiritual being associated with the sky world and the sacred bundles that contain the tribe's most powerful medicine. Cheyenne cosmology recognizes the coyote as a protector figure who stands watch at the boundaries of the camp circle, particularly during the Sun Dance, the most sacred of Cheyenne ceremonies. Unlike the trickster spider Wihio (Veeho) who plays the role of the foolish troublemaker in Cheyenne tales, the coyote guardian is a more serious figure, associated with the Thunder Spirit Nonoma who dwells in the summer sky and brings the life-giving rains. The coyote guardian is particularly connected to the sacred arrows, the Maahotse, which are the most powerful objects in Cheyenne religion, and it is said that the guardian was the first being to discover the arrows hidden in a cave by the culture hero Sweet Medicine
source: Indigenous North American folklore; Coyote is a widespread trickster and culture hero.

name: Coyote Guardian (Burmese)
description: Among the coastal Swahili communities of Kenya and the inland peoples who have traded across the Indian Ocean for centuries, the coyote guardian has evolved from its Burmese origins into a distinctly East African spirit that protects the ancient trade routes connecting the coast to the interior. This spirit reflects the historical connections between Southeast Asia and East Africa through the monsoon trade winds that carried not only spices and textiles but also stories and spiritual beliefs across the Indian Ocean. In Swahili folklore, the coyote guardian is known as the Mlinzi wa Barabara, or Guardian of the Path, and it is invoked by caravan leaders before they set out on journeys into the interior. It is particularly associated with the crossroads where multiple trade routes intersect, places that Swahili tradition considers spiritually potent and deserving of respect and offerings
source: Burmese folklore — guardian spirit from Myanmar oral tradition.

name: Black-Necked Crane Spirit (Thrung Thrung Karmo)
description: In Bhutan, the black-necked crane (Grus nigricollis) is revered as a sacred bird, believed to be the soul of virtuous monks and nuns returned to earth in elegant avian form. The most famous legend says that the cranes circle the Gangteng Monastery in the Phobjikha Valley three times in a clockwise direction upon their arrival each October — a traditional Buddhist circumambulation (kora) that is seen as a profound blessing and affirmation of the sacredness of the valley. The Sixth Dalai Lama, Tsangyang Gyatso (1683–1706), who was also a renowned poet, wrote a famous verse: 'Oh white crane, lend me your wings, I am not going far and away — from Lithang I shall return in a short while.' The cranes are believed to possess awareness of Buddhist astrological calendars, timing their annual migration with remarkable precision. Local farmers consider the arrival of healthy crane numbers a promise of good harvests, and a decline is seen as an omen of hardship. The traditional punishment for killing a black-necked crane is life imprisonment — the strongest legal protection given to any bird in Bhutan. The annual Black-Necked Crane Festival, held on November 11 at Gangteng Monastery, celebrates the cranes' return with schoolchildren performing crane dances in black-and-white costumes
source: RSPN Bhutan, Bhutanese folk traditions, Black-Necked Crane Festival records

name: Lafaek (The Crocodile Prince)
description: Lafaek (The Crocodile Prince) is a central figure in Timor-Leste's foundational creation myth, explaining why the island of Timor is shaped like a crocodile. According to legend, a young boy discovered a baby crocodile struggling to reach the sea and compassionately carried it to the water. The grateful crocodile promised to repay the boy and invited him to ride on its back. Despite its gratitude, the crocodile fought its predatory instinct to eat the boy. Seeking counsel from the whale, tiger, and water buffalo — all of whom said 'you cannot eat him' — and finally a wise monkey who cursed the crocodile, the crocodile resolved to protect the boy. When the crocodile grew old, it offered its body as a gift, transforming into the island of Timor so the boy and his descendants would have a homeland forever. Timor is often called the 'Land of the Sleeping Crocodile.'
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lafaek_Diak

name: Cunjah Maum
description: Cunjah Maum (also spelled Conjure Maum or Conjure Mum) is an archetypal figure in African American folklore — an elderly wise woman who practices conjure and rootwork. 'Maum' is a Gullah/Geechee and African American vernacular term for an older woman (from 'ma'am' or West African linguistic roots). Cunjah Maum is the female counterpart of the Conjure Doctor, serving as the community's spiritual advisor, healer, and protector. She knows the properties of every root, herb, and leaf, can cast spells for protection or revenge, and can identify and counter the work of enemy conjurers. In the Uncle Remus stories and Gullah folktales, she is often sought out by those afflicted by hags or haints. Cunjah Maum represents the preservation and transmission of African spiritual knowledge through generations of women
source: Charles C. Jones, Negro Myths from the Georgia Coast (1888)

name: Čázevulošnieida
description: Čázevulošnieida (the Underwater Girl) is a Sea Sami spirit from the Unjárga/Nesseby region on the Varangerfjord, Norway. She is the daughter of Čáhceháldi (the Sea Guard), a mythical sea ranger who lives in a parallel underwater world. When a Sami fisherman boy encounters her, their meeting reveals how perspectives are completely inverted between the world above the waves and the world below — what is 'up' for one is 'down' for the other. The story originates from the Sea Sami cultural heritage area around Ceavccageađge/Mortensnes, one of the most important Sami cultural heritage sites in Norway. The tale explores themes of parallel worlds, inverted realities, and the meeting of different orders of existence. The story has been adapted into contemporary dance performances and art installations at Black Box teater in Oslo, demonstrating the ongoing vitality of this myth
source: Black Box teater (blackbox.no); BIBU (bibu.se); Sea Sami oral tradition

name: Dab Pog (Spirit Couple of Children)
description: Dab Pog (the Spirit Couple) are the most beloved protective spirits in Hmong folk religion — a celestial husband-and-wife pair responsible for bringing children to parents on earth and protecting them throughout their lives. According to Hmong mythology, at the very beginning of time, the Dab Pog couple and the Xwm Kab (House Spirit) couple were sent by Yawm Saub to live with the Hmong people. The Dab Pog couple resides in the spirit world and decides which souls will be reborn into which families. They guide the child's soul from the spirit world to the mother's womb, and after birth, they serve as the child's guardian angels — protecting them from illness, accidents, and evil spirits. When a child is sick, Hmong parents perform rituals to the Dab Pog couple, asking them to call back the child's wandering soul. The couple is honored with offerings during major life events including births, naming ceremonies, and the Hmong New Year. They represent the deep Hmong belief in spiritual parentage alongside biological parentage
source: Hmong oral tradition — Dab Pog spirit figure.

name: Dakkhin Rai (Tiger Spirit of the Sundarbans)
description: Dakkhin Rai (sometimes spelled Dakshin Rai) is a powerful tiger spirit and demon-king who rules the Sundarbans mangrove forest, the world's largest delta shared between India and Bangladesh. According to Bengali folklore, particularly the Bonbibi tradition, Dakkhin Rai was a shape-shifting tiger demon who demanded human sacrifices from those who entered his forest domain. He is described as the king of the southern region (dakshin meaning south), and his rule extended over the dense, treacherous mangrove forests. He would appear as a man or as a Bengal tiger, using his shapeshifting abilities to deceive and devour honey collectors, woodcutters, and fishermen who entered his territory. According to legend, he was ultimately subdued by the forest goddess Bonbibi and her brother Shah Jangali, who forced him to agree never to harm those who called upon Bonbibi's name. Despite this defeat, Dakkhin Rai continues to be respected and feared — offerings are made to him before entering the forest, and he is considered both a dangerous spirit and a legitimate lord of the Sundarbans ecosystem
source: Bonbibir Gaan (oral ballad tradition), Sundarbans folklore, Mandakranta Bose scholarship

name: De Syv Søstre
description: De Syv Søstre (the Seven Sisters) are the seven daughters of Suliskongen, the troll king of Sulitjelma. According to the famous Helgeland legend cycle, the sisters were sent away from home for discipline and ended up on the island of Alsten. When pursued by Hestmannen, they danced on the shore to distract him, but were caught by the sunrise and turned into the seven peaks that form one of Norway's most iconic mountain silhouettes. The seven peaks, from north to south, are: Botnkrona (youngest), Grytfoten, Skjeringen, Tvillingene (two peaks — the Twins), Kvasstinden, and Breitinden (eldest, who had an illegitimate child — a smaller eighth peak beside her). The Seven Sisters mountain range rises dramatically from the sea near Sandnessjøen. The legend is the best-known folk tale in Northern Norway and the subject of countless songs, poems, and paintings
source: Scandinavian folklore; trolls are pervasive anthropomorphic beings in Nordic myths, documented in laestadian and ethnographic records.

name: De underjordiska (Swedish)
description: De underjordiska (the underground ones) are a hidden, invisible people in Swedish folklore who live parallel to humans in an underground world beneath hills, meadows, and farmyards. They maintain their own farms, cattle, and paths called vitterstigar or onstreck that humans must never obstruct. These beings are most prominent in northern Swedish folklore, where they are often called vittror or vitterfolk, and are closely related to the Norwegian huldrefolk and the Gutnish "di sma undar jordi" (the little ones under the earth). They are generally invisible but can appear to those with second sight, and they are described as small, human-like beings with fair features who lead lives mirroring human existence. Their cattle — vitterkor — are known as particularly fine and productive, giving much more milk than ordinary cows. If a human builds a house or barn on a vitterpath, misfortune follows until the building is moved. Leaving offerings and showing respect ensures their goodwill, while disrespect brings illness, broken tools, and bad luck
source: Swedish folklore

name: Den Grå Dame
description: Den Grå Dame (the Grey Lady) is a famous ghost of Arendal, haunting the Det Kallevigske palé (Kallevig Palace), the old town hall of Arendal. The Grey Lady is the ghost of Cathrine Kitty Kallevig (1783-1840s), a wealthy shipowner's wife who lived in the mansion. Dressed in a grey 1800s silk dress, she has been seen by numerous employees since the 1980s — appearing in the upper-floor hallways, near the grand staircase, and in the council chamber. Her appearances reportedly increased during the 1992 municipal merger when the building was used for contentious political meetings. The Grey Lady is said to be a protective spirit who watches over the building. Local historians note that the tradition contains elements from international castle ghost traditions adapted to the Sørlandet setting. Academic studies have compared her to the Grey Lady of Glamis and other European grey lady traditions
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Devi
description: Devi is the great goddess in Hinduism, embodying the supreme feminine divine energy known as Shakti. Worshipped across India for millennia, she manifests in both benevolent and fearsome forms. As the mother goddess Mahadevi, she is the source of all creation, preservation, and destruction. Her gentle aspect appears as Parvati, Uma, and Gauri — the loving consort of Shiva. Her fierce aspect manifests as Durga, the ten-armed warrior goddess who rides a lion into battle against demons, and Kali, the black goddess of time and destruction who wears a garland of skulls. The Devi Mahatmya, a sacred text from the Markandeya Purana, recounts her epic battles against the buffalo demon Mahishasura and the demon lords Shumbha and Nishumbha, establishing her as the supreme protectress of cosmic order In India folklore, this figure is known among the India people.
source: Indian folklore — ogress documented in Indian oral tradition.

name: Devil's Tower
description: Devil's Tower, known as Mato Tipila or Bear Lodge to the Lakota and Tso-aa to the Kiowa, is a sacred geological formation in northeastern Wyoming and the first declared United States National Monument. In the oral traditions of over twenty Native American tribes including the Lakota, Cheyenne, Kiowa, Crow, and Arapaho, this 1,267-foot monolith of striated igneous rock is a living spiritual being central to creation narratives. The most widespread legend tells of seven young girls chased by a giant bear who climbed onto a low rock and prayed for deliverance. The Great Spirit caused the rock to grow skyward, carrying the girls beyond the bear's reach. The bear's claws scored the rock's sides, creating the distinctive vertical columns visible today. The girls became the constellation Pleiades. The Tower remains a site of vision quests, prayer offerings, and ceremonial bundles left among its crevices
source: Lakota spiritual tradition; documented in Plains indigenous records.

name: Dewi Sri (Rice Goddess)
description: Dewi Sri is the revered Javanese, Sundanese, and Balinese Hindu goddess of rice and fertility, still widely worshipped across Indonesia. According to Sundanese myth, she was born from a miraculous egg laid by the naga god Antaboga. She grew into a princess of such beauty that the supreme god Batara Guru became dangerously attracted to her. To prevent scandal in heaven, the gods poisoned her, and her innocent body was buried. From her grave sprouted all the useful plants essential to humanity: from her head grew coconuts, from her eyes grew rice (white from the right, red from the left), from her hair grew grasses, from her arms grew teak trees, and from her body grew all fruits, vegetables, and tubers. She is equated with the Hindu goddess Lakshmi and remains the most important agricultural deity in Indonesia
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewi_Sri

name: Dhanvantari (Physician of the Gods)
description: Dhanvantari is the Hindu god of medicine and the physician of the gods (devas), revered as the originator of Ayurveda, the ancient Indian system of medicine. He emerged from the churning of the Ocean of Milk (Samudra Manthana) holding a pot of amrita (the nectar of immortality) in his hands. According to the Bhagavata Purana and Vishnu Purana, Dhanvantari rose from the ocean as the last of the fourteen treasures (ratnas), carrying the pot of nectar that the devas and asuras had been churning for. He is considered an avatar of Vishnu, appearing to restore health and longevity to the world. The name Dhanvantari means 'moving like a bow' or 'one who travels through the arc of a bow,' referring to the swift and direct nature of his healing. He is credited with compiling the Ayurvedic text the Charaka Samhita in some traditions, though Charaka is more commonly identified as the primary author. Dhanvantari is worshipped by physicians, surgeons, and those seeking healing
source: Bhagavata Purana, Vishnu Purana, Atharvaveda, Ayurvedic texts
